title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Hydrostatics, Pascal's Law, Buoyancy, Archimedes' Principle, Equation of Continuity, Bernoulli's Theorem, Torricelli's Law, Viscosity, Stokes' Law & Surface Tension
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Makes a Fluid Different from a Solid?

Imagine pushing your hand against a block of solid wood. The wood resists your hand and keeps its shape because its atoms are locked into a rigid lattice. Now push your hand into water. The water parts around your hand and flows. Why?

A Fluid is any substance that can flow—which includes both liquids and gases. Unlike solids, which resist sideways (shear) forces by deforming up to an elastic limit, fluids have molecules that slide freely past one another. A fluid at rest cannot sustain any tangential shear stress; the moment a sideways force acts on it, layers begin to slide.

The 4 Pillars of Fluid Mechanics in This Chapter:
  • 1. Hydrostatics (Fluids at Rest): Pressure variation with depth ($P = P_0 + \rho gh$), barometer/manometer tubes, Pascal's hydraulic lift, and Archimedes' buoyancy ($F_b = V_{\text{sub}}\rho_L g$).
  • 2. Hydrodynamics (Ideal Fluids in Motion): Conservation of mass ($A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$) and conservation of energy (Bernoulli's equation, Torricelli's efflux speed, Venturi meter, and dynamic lift).
  • 3. Viscosity (Internal Fluid Friction): Velocity gradient, Poiseuille's tube flow, Stokes' drag on a sphere ($F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$), and Terminal Velocity ($v_T$).
  • 4. Surface Tension & Capillarity: Molecular origin of surface energy ($S = F/L = U/\Delta A$), angle of contact, excess pressure inside drops ($2S/R$) and soap bubbles ($4S/R$), and Jurin's capillary rise law.

topics.title: Hydrostatic Pressure, Pascal's Law, Accelerated Containers, Buoyancy & Archimedes' Principle
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Fluid Pressure & Density
Definition of Pressure ($P$):
The normal (perpendicular) thrust force exerted by a fluid per unit surface area is called Pressure. At any point inside a static fluid, pressure acts equally in all directions, so Pressure is a Scalar quantity.
$$\boxed{P = \frac{dF_{\perp}}{dA}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Density } \rho = \frac{\text{Mass } (m)}{\text{Volume } (V)} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Relative Density (Specific Gravity)} = \frac{\rho_{\text{substance}}}{\rho_{\text{water at } 4^\circ\text{C}}}$$

Standard Pressure Units: SI unit is $\text{Pascal (Pa)} = \text{N/m}^2$. Also $1\text{ atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\text{ Pa} = 76\text{ cm of Hg} = 760\text{ Torr}$, and $1\text{ bar} = 10^5\text{ Pa}$.

1.2 Variation of Pressure with Depth, Gauge Pressure & Pascal's Law
$$\text{Absolute Pressure at Depth } h: \quad \boxed{P = P_0 + \rho g h} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Gauge Pressure:} \quad \boxed{P_g = P - P_0 = \rho g h}$$
Pascal's Law:
Any external pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and the walls of the vessel. In a hydraulic lift with small piston area $A_1$ and large piston area $A_2$:
$$\boxed{\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2} \implies F_2 = \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)F_1} \qquad \text{while Work Conserved:} \quad F_1 y_1 = F_2 y_2$$

Liquid in an Accelerating Container:
1. Vertical upward acceleration $a_0$: Effective gravity becomes $g_{\text{eff}} = g + a_0 \implies P = P_0 + \rho(g + a_0)h$.
2. Horizontal acceleration $a_x$: The free surface of the liquid tilts backward making an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal such that:

$$\boxed{\tan\theta = \frac{a_x}{g}} \qquad \text{and pressure difference along horizontal length } L \text{ is } \Delta P = \rho a_x L$$
1.3 Buoyancy & Archimedes' Principle
Archimedes' Principle:
When a body of volume $V$ and density $\rho_B$ is wholly or partially submerged in a liquid of density $\rho_L$, the fluid exerts an upward Buoyant Force (Upthrust $F_b$) equal to the weight of the displaced liquid, acting upward through the Center of Buoyancy (centroid of the displaced volume).
$$\boxed{F_b = V_{\text{sub}} \rho_L g} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Apparent Weight in Liquid:} \quad W_{\text{app}} = W_{\text{air}}\left(1 - \frac{\rho_L}{\rho_B}\right)$$
$$\textbf{Law of Floatation } (\rho_B < \rho_L): \quad m_B g = F_b \implies V_{\text{total}} \rho_B g = V_{\text{sub}} \rho_L g \implies \boxed{\frac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V_{\text{total}}} = \frac{\rho_B}{\rho_L}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1: Hydrostatic Pressure P = P₀ + ρgh

Consider an imaginary vertical cylinder of liquid of cross-sectional area $A$ extending from the top surface ($y = 0$, pressure $P_0$) to depth $h$ (pressure $P$). Since the liquid cylinder is in vertical equilibrium:

$$\text{Upward Force from Bottom} = \text{Downward Force at Top} + \text{Weight of Liquid Cylinder}$$$$P A = P_0 A + (\rho A h)g \implies \boxed{P = P_0 + \rho g h}$$
Derivation 2: Free-Surface Tilt Angle tan(θ) = aₓ / g in Horizontally Accelerating Tank

Take a small fluid parcel of mass $m$ right on the tilted free surface from the non-inertial frame of the tank. It experiences downward gravity $mg$ and backward pseudo force $ma_x$. Since a static free surface must be perpendicular to the net effective force vector, the tangent of the tilt angle $\theta$ with the horizontal is:

$$\boxed{\tan\theta = \frac{m a_x}{m g} = \frac{a_x}{g}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Hydrostatic Paradox): Three vessels of completely different shapes (cone, cylinder, flared funnel) having the same base area $A$ and filled with water to the same height $h$ experience the exact same force on their base ($F = P A = (P_0 + \rho gh)A$), even though the weight of water inside them is different! The side walls supply the remaining vertical reaction force.
  • Trap 2 (Ice Melting in a Glass of Water): When a block of pure ice floating in water melts completely, the water level in the glass remains strictly unchanged! If the ice contains a heavy coin or stone (which sinks to the bottom after melting), the water level falls!

topics.title: Hydrodynamics: Equation of Continuity, Bernoulli's Theorem, Torricelli's Efflux Law & Venturi Meter
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Streamline vs. Turbulent Flow & Equation of Continuity
Streamline (Laminar) Flow:
A flow in which every fluid particle passing a given point follows the exact same path and has the exact same velocity as the preceding particle. Two streamlines can never intersect!
$$\textbf{Equation of Continuity (Conservation of Mass):} \quad \boxed{A_1 \rho_1 v_1 = A_2 \rho_2 v_2} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Incompressible}} \quad \boxed{Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = \text{Constant}}$$
2.2 Bernoulli's Theorem (Conservation of Mechanical Energy per Unit Volume)
Statement:
For the steady, irrotational, streamline flow of an ideal (incompressible and non-viscous) fluid, the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume remains constant along a streamline.
$$\boxed{P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{Constant}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Head Form:} \quad \frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{v^2}{2g} + h = \text{Constant}$$
2.3 Torricelli's Law of Efflux & Horizontal Range of Escaping Jet

Consider a wide tank filled with liquid to total height $H$. A small hole of area $a \ll A$ is made in the side wall at depth $h$ below the free surface (so height of the hole above the ground is $y = H - h$):

$$\text{1. Speed of Efflux:} \quad \boxed{v = \sqrt{2gh}} \qquad \left(\text{Exact for large hole: } v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 - (a/A)^2}}\right)$$
$$\text{2. Time to Hit Ground:} \quad t = \sqrt{\frac{2(H - h)}{g}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{3. Horizontal Range:} \quad \boxed{R = v t = 2\sqrt{h(H - h)}}$$

Maximum Range Condition: $R$ is maximum when $h = H - h \implies \boxed{h = \frac{H}{2}}$ (hole exactly at mid-height of the liquid column), giving $\boxed{R_{\max} = H}$!
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation & Venturi Meter Flow Speed

1. Bernoulli's Equation: For a volume $\Delta V = A_1 v_1 \Delta t = A_2 v_2 \Delta t$ of mass $\Delta m = \rho \Delta V$ moving from section 1 to section 2, Work-Energy Theorem ($W_{\text{pressure}} + W_{\text{gravity}} = \Delta K$) gives:

$$(P_1 - P_2)\Delta V - \rho \Delta V g(h_2 - h_1) = \frac{1}{2}\rho \Delta V (v_2^2 - v_1^2) \implies \boxed{P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho gh_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho gh_2}$$

2. Venturi Meter (Horizontal Pipe with Constriction $A_2 < A_1$):
Since $h_1 = h_2$, $P_1 - P_2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_2^2 - v_1^2) = \rho g \Delta h$. Substituting $v_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2}v_1$ gives:

$$\boxed{v_1 = A_2 \sqrt{\frac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho(A_1^2 - A_2^2)}} = A_2 \sqrt{\frac{2gh_m}{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Rocket-Like Reaction Thrust of Escaping Liquid Jet): When water squirts out of a hole of area $a$ at speed $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, mass leaves at rate $\frac{dm}{dt} = \rho a v$. This exerts a backward reaction thrust force on the tank of magnitude $\boxed{F_{\text{thrust}} = v\frac{dm}{dt} = \rho a v^2 = 2\rho a g h}$ (notice the factor of $2$, NOT $\rho a g h$!).
  • Trap 2 (Maximum Range Depends Only on $H$, Not on $g$ or $\rho$!): Since $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$, both density $\rho$ and gravity $g$ cancel out completely! On the Moon, the water squirts out slower, but it also takes longer to fall, so it lands at the exact same horizontal distance $R$!

topics.title: Viscosity, Poiseuille's Formula, Reynolds Number, Stokes' Law & Terminal Velocity
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Newton's Law of Viscosity & Poiseuille's Capillary Flow
Velocity Gradient ($\frac{dv}{dz}$):
When a viscous fluid flows over a fixed horizontal plate, the bottom layer in contact with the plate is stationary ($v = 0$), and each higher layer moves faster. The rate of change of velocity with perpendicular distance $z$ is called the Velocity Gradient.
$$\text{Viscous Force:} \quad \boxed{F = -\eta A \frac{dv}{dz}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{SI Unit of } \eta: \; 1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s} = 1\text{ decapoise} = 10\text{ Poise}$$

Poiseuille's Formula (Volume Flow Rate through a Cylindrical Pipe of Radius $r$ and Length $L$):

$$\boxed{Q = \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{\pi P r^4}{8 \eta L} = \frac{\Delta P}{R_{\text{fluid}}}} \qquad \left(\text{where Fluid Resistance } R_{\text{fluid}} = \frac{8\eta L}{\pi r^4}\right)$$
3.2 Stokes' Law & Terminal Velocity ($v_T$)
$$\text{Stokes' Viscous Drag on a Sphere of Radius } r: \quad \boxed{F_v = 6\pi \eta r v}$$
$$\text{Terminal Velocity of Sphere } (\text{density } \rho \text{ in fluid of density } \sigma): \quad \boxed{v_T = \frac{2 r^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta}}$$

Coalescence of $N$ Identical Drops (High-Frequency JEE Formula!):
If $N$ identical small droplets (each of radius $r$ and terminal speed $v_T$) merge to form 1 big drop of radius $R$, volume conservation gives $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = N\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) \implies \mathbf{R = N^{1/3}r}$. Since $v_T \propto r^2$:

$$\boxed{v_{T,\text{big}} = N^{2/3} v_{T,\text{small}}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Terminal Velocity & Exponential Approach v(t)

1. Terminal Velocity ($a = 0$): Equating downward weight $W = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ to upward buoyancy $F_b = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \sigma g$ plus Stokes drag $6\pi\eta r v_T$:

$$\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (\rho - \sigma)g = 6\pi\eta r v_T \implies \boxed{v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}}$$

2. Velocity as a Function of Time before Reaching Terminal Speed:

$$m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg_{\text{eff}} - 6\pi\eta r v \implies \boxed{v(t) = v_T\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)} \quad \left(\text{where } \tau = \frac{m}{6\pi\eta r}\right)$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Air Bubble Rising in Water — Negative $\rho - \sigma$): If an air bubble ($\rho_{\text{air}} \approx 0$) is inside water of density $\sigma$, then $\rho - \sigma < 0$, which means its terminal velocity is upward with magnitude $v_T = \frac{2r^2 \sigma g}{9\eta}$!
  • Trap 2 (Poiseuille's $r^4$ Sensitivity): Because volume flow rate $Q \propto r^4$, halving the radius of an artery or capillary pipe reduces the flow rate to $\frac{1}{16}$ of its original value (or requires $16\times$ more pressure difference)!

topics.title: Surface Tension, Surface Energy, Excess Pressure in Drops/Bubbles & Capillary Rise
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Surface Tension ($S$) & Surface Energy ($U$)
Definition:
Surface Tension ($S$) is the tangential force per unit length acting on either side of an imaginary line drawn on the free liquid surface, tending to minimize the surface area. Equivalently, it equals the Surface Energy per unit area:
$$\boxed{S = \frac{F}{L} = \frac{\text{Work Done } (W)}{\text{Increase in Free Surface Area } (\Delta A)}} \qquad \left(\text{SI Unit: } \text{N/m} = \text{J/m}^2, \; [M^1 L^0 T^{-2}]\right)$$
4.2 Excess Pressure Inside Liquid Drops & Soap Bubbles
SystemFree SurfacesSurface Area $\Delta A$Excess Pressure ($P_{\text{in}} - P_{\text{out}}$)
1. Liquid Drop in Air1 (Outer only)$4\pi R^2$$$\Delta P = \frac{2S}{R}$$
2. Air Bubble Inside Liquid1 (Inner only)$4\pi R^2$$$\Delta P = \frac{2S}{R}$$
3. Soap Bubble in Air2 (Inner & Outer)$2 \times (4\pi R^2) = 8\pi R^2$$$\Delta P = \frac{4S}{R}$$

Two Soap Bubbles in Contact (Radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ with $R_1 < R_2$):
1. When connected by a tube, air flows from the smaller bubble ($R_1$, higher pressure $4S/R_1$) into the larger bubble ($R_2$, lower pressure $4S/R_2$)!
2. When two bubbles touch and share a common interface film, the radius of curvature $R_c$ of the common interface is:

$$\frac{4S}{R_c} = \frac{4S}{R_1} - \frac{4S}{R_2} \implies \boxed{R_c = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_2 - R_1}}$$
4.3 Capillarity & Jurin's Law (Tube of Insufficient Length)
$$\text{Capillary Rise / Depression:} \quad \boxed{h = \frac{2S\cos\theta}{r\rho g} = \frac{2S}{R_{\text{meniscus}}\rho g}} \qquad \left(\text{where } R_{\text{meniscus}} = \frac{r}{\cos\theta}\right)$$

Jurin's Law for a Tube of Insufficient Length ($L < h$):
Since $h \cdot R_{\text{meniscus}} = \frac{2S}{\rho g} = \text{Constant}$, if a capillary tube is cut to a height $h' < h$, liquid NEVER overflows like a fountain! Instead, the liquid rises to the top rim $h'$ and the meniscus flattens out to a larger radius $R'$ such that $\boxed{h' R' = h R_{\text{meniscus}}} \implies h' \cos\theta = h \cos\theta'$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Virtual Work Proof of Excess Pressure inside a Soap Bubble (ΔP = 4S/R)

Suppose excess pressure $\Delta P = P_{\text{in}} - P_{\text{out}}$ expands a soap bubble of radius $R$ by a tiny radial distance $dR$:

Step 1 (Work done by excess pressure): $dW = F\,dR = (\Delta P \cdot 4\pi R^2)dR$.

Step 2 (Increase in surface energy of 2 free surfaces): Total area is $A = 2(4\pi R^2) = 8\pi R^2$, so $dA = 16\pi R\,dR$, and $dU = S\,dA = S(16\pi R\,dR)$.

Step 3 (Equate $dW = dU$):

$$(\Delta P \cdot 4\pi R^2)dR = 16\pi S R\,dR \implies \boxed{\Delta P = \frac{4S}{R}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Sliding Wire on a Soap Film Frame — Factor of $2L$): A thin wire of length $L$ sliding on a U-shaped frame dipped in soap solution has two liquid-air surfaces (front and back), so the surface tension force pulling the wire is $\mathbf{F = 2SL}$, NOT $SL$!
  • Trap 2 (Energy Released vs. Absorbed in Splitting/Merging Drops):
    • Splitting 1 big drop of radius $R$ into $N$ small droplets ($r = R/N^{1/3}$): Total surface area increases, so work must be done ON the drop (heat is absorbed, temperature drops): $W = 4\pi R^2 S (N^{1/3} - 1)$.
    • Merging $N$ small droplets into 1 big drop: Total surface area decreases, so energy is released as heat (temperature rises): $\Delta E = 4\pi R^2 S (N^{1/3} - 1)$.

conclusion: You have completed Chapter 09: Mechanical Properties of Fluids with full conceptual and mathematical depth! Every single equation—from hydrostatics and Bernoulli's energy law to Stokes' drag and capillarity—is ready for JEE Main and Advanced numericals.
summary:
• Hydrostatics: $P = P_0 + \rho gh$; Free surface tilt $\tan\theta = a_x/g$; Buoyancy $F_b = V_{\text{sub}}\rho_L g$.
  • Hydrodynamics: Continuity $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$; Bernoulli $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{const}$; Torricelli $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$.
  • Viscosity: $F = -\eta A\frac{dv}{dz}$; Poiseuille $Q = \frac{\pi P r^4}{8\eta L}$; Stokes $F_v = 6\pi\eta r v$; Terminal speed $v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}$.
  • Surface Tension: $S = F/L = W/\Delta A$; Drop $\Delta P = 2S/R$; Soap bubble $\Delta P = 4S/R$; Capillary rise $h = \frac{2S\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$.

questions.prompt: A wooden block floats in water with $\frac{3}{5}$ of its volume submerged. When placed in an unknown oil, it floats with $\frac{3}{4}$ of its volume submerged. What is the density of the oil? ($\rho_{\text{water}} = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$)
questions.explanation: By the Law of Floatation, $\frac{V_{\text{sub}}}{V} = \frac{\rho_B}{\rho_L}$. In water: $\rho_B = \frac{3}{5}(1000) = 600\text{ kg/m}^3$. In oil: $\frac{3}{4} = \frac{600}{\rho_{\text{oil}}} \implies \rho_{\text{oil}} = \frac{4}{3}(600) = 800\text{ kg/m}^3$.

questions.prompt: The radius of a soap bubble is doubled from $R$ to $2R$. By what factor does the excess pressure inside the soap bubble change?
questions.explanation: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble is $\Delta P = \frac{4S}{R} \propto \frac{1}{R}$. Doubling the radius halves the excess pressure.

questions.prompt: A cylindrical tank of height $H = 6.25\text{ m}$ is open at the top and filled completely with water. A small hole is punched in the side wall at a height of $1.25\text{ m}$ from the bottom. With what speed does the water jet emerge? ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.explanation: Depth of the hole below the free water surface is $h = H - y = 6.25 - 1.25 = 5.0\text{ m}$. By Torricelli's Law, $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(10)(5.0)} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ m/s}$.

questions.prompt: A small spherical drop of water of radius $r$ falls freely in air and reaches a terminal velocity $v$. If $27$ such identical drops coalesce to form a single large drop, what will be the terminal velocity of the large drop?

A mercury drop of radius $R = 1\text{ cm}$ is sprayed into $10^6$ droplets of equal size. If the surface tension of mercury is $S = 0.46\text{ N/m}$, the work done (energy expended) in splitting the drop is:
Two soap bubbles of radii $R_1 = 3\text{ cm}$ and $R_2 = 4\text{ cm}$ coalesce in vacuum under isothermal conditions to form a single bigger bubble of radius $R$. What is the value of $R$?
questions.explanation: In vacuum ($P_0 = 0$), pressure inside a soap bubble is $P = \frac{4S}{R}$ and volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$. By ideal gas mole conservation at constant temperature ($n_1 + n_2 = n \implies P_1 V_1 + P_2 V_2 = PV$): $\left(\frac{4S}{R_1}\right)R_1^3 + \left(\frac{4S}{R_2}\right)R_2^3 = \left(\frac{4S}{R}\right)R^3 \implies R^2 = R_1^2 + R_2^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 25 \implies R = 5\text{ cm}$.

questions.prompt: Water rises to a height $h = 10\text{ cm}$ in a vertical glass capillary tube of zero contact angle ($\theta = 0^\circ$). If the tube is now cut so that only a length $h' = 5\text{ cm}$ projects above the free water surface, what angle $\theta'$ will the water meniscus make with the wall at the top rim?
questions.explanation: By Jurin's adjustment rule for a short capillary tube, $h'\cos\theta' = h\cos\theta \implies 5\cos\theta' = 10\cos(0^\circ) \dots$ Wait: the radius of curvature of the meniscus increases from $R = r$ to $R' = 2r$, where $r = R'\cos\theta'$. Thus $\frac{h'}{h} = \frac{\cos\theta'}{\cos\theta} \implies \cos\theta' = \frac{5}{10}(1) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \theta' = 60^\circ$.

questions.prompt: A large open tank is filled with water to a height $H$. A small hole of cross-sectional area $a$ is punched at the base of the tank. If the static friction coefficient between the tank (total mass $M$) and the horizontal floor is $\mu$, what is the minimum value of $\mu$ so that the tank does not start sliding backward due to the escaping jet?
questions.explanation: Efflux speed at base is $v = \sqrt{2gH}$. The backward reaction thrust force of the jet is $F_{\text{thrust}} = \rho a v^2 = 2\rho a g H$. For no sliding, $F_{\text{thrust}} \le \mu M g \implies 2\rho a g H \le \mu M g \implies \mu_{\min} = \frac{2\rho a H}{M}$.
